A LIVELY CHASE.
Two Police Officers Attempt to Catch an Escaped Convict—Four Shots Fired.
Two Police Officers Attempt to Catch an Escaped Convict—Four Shots Fired.

Officers Culpepper and Whalen gave a negro, who was an escaped convict from Coalburg, a lively chase last night at 11 o'clock. The negro was Andrew Mills, alias Dago Bill, and was recognized by the above named officers as he was standing on Alley D and Twentieth street. As soon as he saw them he turned to run, and Officer Culpepper, who knew the negro, hailed him and ordered him to halt. The order was not heeded, and a chase opened up. As Officer Culpepper was running he fired two shots at the negro, thinking to stop him, and while so doing fell and injured his knee cap.

Officer Whalen then took up the chase and followed the fleeing negro to Seventeenth street, and also fired two shots at him, but the negro escaped.

THE WRONG MAN.
Ford, Ky., July 28.—It has developed that the negro, Bob Haggard, who was lynched here last week, charged with having outraged Miss Elkin, was innocent of the crime with which he was charged. The story told of how the deed was done has been proven to be utterly false. Haggard admitted that he had been intimate with the girl, but said he had never assaulted her. The work was done by a few hot-headed men who did not take time to inquire whether Haggard was guilty or not.

Lynched an Innocent Man.

FORD, Ky., July 29.—It developed Friday that the negro, Bob Haggard, who was lynched here last week, charged with having outraged Miss Elkin, was innocent of the crime with which he was charged. The story told of how the deed was done has been proven to be utterly false. The work was done by a few hot-headed men who did not take time to inquire whether Haggard was guilty or not.

How Icebergs Break From Glaciers.

The number of bergs given off varies somewhat with the weather and the tides, the average being about one every five or six minutes, counting only those large enough to thunder loudly, and make themselves heard at a distance of two or three miles. The very largest, however, may, under favorable conditions, be heard ten miles, or even farther. When a large mass sinks from the upper fissured portion of the wall, there is first a keen, piercing crash, then a deep, deliberate, prolonged, thundering roar, which slowly subsides into a low, muttering growl, followed by numerous smaller, grating, clashing sounds from the agitated bergs that dance in the waves about the newcomer as if in welcome; and these again are followed by the swash and roar of the waves that are raised and hurled against the moraines. But the largest and most beautiful of the bergs, instead of thus falling from the upper weathered portion of the wall, rise from the submerged portion with a still grander commotion, springing with tremendous voice and gestures nearly to the top of the wall, tons of water streaming like hair down their sides, plunging and rising again and again before they finally settle in perfect poise, free at last, after having formed part of a slow-crawling glacier for centuries.—John Muir, in Century.

LEGEND OF PIKE'S PEAK. Strange Belief of the Indians About the Great Mountain's Origin. While the geological and mineralog
While the geological and mineralogical history of Pike's Peak is interesting, the real story of the place comes from the Indian legends. To Ernest Whitney, of Colorado Springs, belongs the credit of discovering these legends and in a certain measure preserving them. Mr. Whitney is a Howard graduate, and when he went to Colorado many years ago he became greatly interested in the Indian traditions. He devoted years to his study of them, and has visited nearly every tribe in the country on its reservation in search of information. His hardest work was to separate the old Indian legend from the interpolations which were the result of intercourse with the whites. His work was conscientiously done, and although many interesting features are omitted as being apocryphal, the legends as given to-day are the identical legends which were told in the tribes two hundred and fifty years ago.

Mr. Whitney is convinced that centuries ago there was a close connection between the mountain tribes of Indians and the Aztecs, but says he had no conclusive proof. The Indian legends, especially the account of the flood, which is a factor in the legends of all savage races, will prove of interest to the Bible scholar who will compare it with his book of Genesis.

The legend of the formation of Pike's Peak, as given by Mr. Whitney, follows: "At the beginning of all things the Lesser Spirits possessed the earth and dwelt near the banks of the Great river. They had created a race of men to be their servants, but these men were far superior to the present inhabitants of the earth and made endless trouble for their creators. Therefore the lesser spirits resolved to destroy mankind and the earth itself; so they caused the Great river to rise till it burst its banks and overwhelmed everything. They themselves took each a large portion of the best of the earth that they might create a new world, and a quantity of maize, which had been their particular food, and returned to Heaven. Arriving at the gate of Heaven, which is at the end of the plains, where the sky and mountains meet, they were told that they could not bring such burdens of earth into Heaven. Accordingly they dropped them all then and there. These falling masses made a great heap on the top of the world which extended far above the waters, and this is the origin of Pike's Peak, which is thus shown to be directly under the gate of Heaven. [It was formerly twice as high as now, but lost its summit, as is told in another legend.]

"The rock masses upon it and all about show that they have been dropped from the sky. The variety and extent of the mineral wealth in the region prove that the earth's choicest materials are deposited there. And still as the constellations move across the heavens and vanish above the mountain summits we may see the spirits rise from the Great river and pass to the gate of Heaven. The falling stars are their falling burdens or the drooping grains of maize."—Chicago Times-Herald.

It is proposed that a parade of confederate veterans, under command of lien, Buckner, shall be reviewed by the A. R. commander-in-chief during the encampment at Louisville.

Geo. RORINSON, keeper of the Meade county poorhouse, was killed a few days ago by Blanton Shacklett.

New post offices established in Kentucky a few days ago: Post, Grayson county, Annie Whitworth appointed postmaster, and Turner, Pendleton county, Mary J. Blackburn appointed postmaster.

There were rumors at Winchester the other day that Bob Hazzard, the Negro lynched recently, on suspicion of having assaulted Miss Elkins, was innocent.

Courtney Slack, a brakeman on the Louisville and Nashville railroad, was killed at Guthrie. His remains were taken to Madisonville for burial.

Mike Brophy, sent up from Louisville to the Frankfort prison for murder, has been respited for ninety days by Gov. Brown. The prison physician says Brophy is dying.

The South Point watermelon growers are complaining of the dry weather of late, and it is reported that the crop will hardly be up to the average in consequence.

The family of Philip Moutz, of Henderson, was poisoned by eating diseased meat. Two of the youngest children, it is now thought, can not recover. The father killed a cow which had some unnatural growth on her side, and the family partook of the meat.

James Murray, of Tolu, is hunting for his wife. She ran away from him a few days ago, and he was only able to trace her to Marion, where he lost the trail.

The state board of health has declared a quarantine against cattle from Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Texas and Indian territory, on account of the reported prevalence of Texas fever.

UNDER the game laws it is unlawful to shoot doves till after August 1. Offenders are liable to a fine of from $5 to $25 for each offense.

THE Henderson city council has let the contract for the laying of over a mile of water mains.

ROSA GORDON, who cut to death Mary Sullivan and Lizzie Brown, at Corbin, is of respectable parentage. She began a life of shame at 13, and is only 16 now.

PATENTS were granted to Kentuckians the other day as follows: Jonathan Creech, Paint Lick, sliding bar for fences. Alexander D. Ruff, Owingsville, cyclometer; James Taylor, Louisville, safety stop for elevators.

THE farmers, having about finished harvesting wheat and having their corn laid by, are now in a position to take a little rest.

A six-year-old boy of McClelland Watt was thrown from a horse at Valley View and killed.

Mormon elders are working at several points in Kentucky.

The post office at Branham, Pike county, will be discontinued after July 31.

At Brownsville at an examining trial the other day Willie, the 12-year-old son of Will Hare Skaggs charged with false swearing, was held for trial at circuit court. His bond was fixed at $100, which was not given. He is the boy who tried to swear away the life of his father.

All streams in the vicinity of Danville were rising rapidly the other day, as a result of the heavy rains. Chaplin river is out of its banks at Perryville.

BUCK MCFARLAND, colored, who killed James Davis and seriously injured Shelby Hayden, was dismissed at Owensboro, on examining trial, a clear case of self-defense having been established.

COL HARVEY PARKER, founder of the Deposit bank of Vanceburg, who had his pension cut in two a few weeks ago, has been restored. Ex-Senator J. P. Huff, who had his pension divided, has also been restored.

PROF. METZ, of the Central Park museum, New York, is in charge of the mound-diggers near Mayslick, Mason county. At a depth of six feet an old corn cob was found, showing that the mound-builders raised maise. A dog's head was also found in a state of good preservation.

THERE were two killings in Pike county the other day, and both are said to have been in self-defense. The victims were Will Thoacker and Jim Coleman, and the slayers were John Matney and Jake Smith.

JIM DAVIS and Shelby Hayden tried to break up a Negro church social at Owensboro by firing pistols at the master of ceremonies, Buck McFarland. McFarland beat both with a club so severely that they died.

MISS MARY DOYLE committed suicide near North Middletown by taking a dose of strychnine. No cause is given.

Lady Henry Somerset is in hard lines. For years she has been advocating temperance and has been handicapped in her work by the widely circulated statements, whose truth she could not deny, that many of her tenements were licensed public houses where liquor was sold. She could only make the defense that she inherited the leases with the property and could make no change until time when the licenses were to be renewed. Now, it appears that she cannot even do this. She holds the estate only as a tenant for life, and the Chancery Court forbids her to allow her personal opinions to affect her actions in her fiduciary capacity. By refusing to lease to liquor dealers it is held that she is likely to impair the incomes and consequently the permanent value of the property, and so jeopardize the interests of the heirs. Henceforth, therefore, she will occupy the amalous position

of teaching temperance by precept and encouraging intemperance by practice. It will not be possible for her to keep her left hand in ignorance of what her right hand does, and the probability is that her usefulness as a temperance teacher will be greatly lessened. She can only take refuge in the feminine conclusion that the law is a mean, hateful thing—which is more refined than Mr. Bumble's verdict, but means the same.

A NEW INTERNATIONAL COMPLICATION.

A Los Angeles, Cal., dispatch in the Journal of yesterday stated that Baron Harden-Hickey, sole proprietor of the Island of Trinidad, was in that city, and had stated his determination to hold on to the island at all hazards. He intimated that Brazil had no more title to it than England had, and that the really important question was what position the United States would take.

This Trinidad question is becoming very complicated. First it was stated that England had occupied the island, then that Brazil had protested against her doing so, and now comes Baron Harden-Hickey and asserts a prior right to both. The Baron seems to be an interesting character. To begin with, he is not a Baron at all, but a French-Irishman, formerly known in New York as James Harden-Hickey. About two years ago he sent word to all the powers that he had taken possession of the uninhabited Island of Trinidad, and intended to establish a principality there and reign under the title of James I. Later on he appointed a Frenchman named Boissiere Grand Chancellor and Secretary for Foreign Affairs of the principality, with the title of count, and with headquarters at New York city, where he now is. James I and his high chancellor constitute the present government of Trinidad. The grand chancellory in New York is in a room on the ground floor of an unpretentious brick tenement house, and contains furniture of the aggregate value of about two dollars. Amid these severely simple environments the Grand Chancellor keeps a sharp lookout for the interests of his august sovereign, James I. A few days ago, when it was announced that England had taken possession of the island, the Grand Chancellor addressed a communication to Secretary of State Olney, at Washington, in which he made the following appeal:

I beg of your Excellency to ask of the government of the United States of North America to recognize the principality of Trinidad as an independent state, and to come to an understanding with the other American powers in order to guarantee its neutrality.

Thus, the government of the United States of North America will once more accord its powerful assistance to the cause of right and of justice, misunderstood by England and Brazil, put an end to a situation which threatens to disturb the peace, re-establish concord between two great states ready to appeal to arms and affirm itself, moreover, as the faithful interpreter of the Monroe doctrine.

In the expectation of your reply, please accept, Excellency, the expression of my elevated consideration.

The Grand Chancellor, Secretary for Foreign Affairs,

It is the Grand Chancellor's intention to follow up this appeal by a personal visit to Washington. He says if England simply wants to land a cable or establish a coaling station on the island, there will be no objection if the rights of the principality are observed, including the recognition of James I as one of the powers; otherwise there will be trouble. Hung an Innocent Man.

The lynching which occurred at Winchester, Ky., one day last week has turned out to be another case of "I told you so." A colored man named Haggard was accused of committing an assault upon a girl and without giving a chance for any explanation, a mob of blue bloods dragged the negro from jail and hung hiu to a bridge. His death was a most fearful one, as he was let down and slowly strangled to death. Fifteen minutes had elapse before the body ceased to show signs of life. Now it develops that there was no assault committed, and the daily press says that the leaders have actually said they are sorry it occurred. That is lots of consolation for a man who is let to heaven with a rope around his neck, and when it's all over, to hear some one say he feels sorry for him. Winchester is in Kentucky, gentlemen, and we have never seen the place.—[Cannelton Enquirer.

At this season of the year, when so many people go to to the seashore and lake shore to escape the summer heat that is so general in the interior country, attention is called to the provision made by the United States government for the preservation of life and property of those who do business on the great waters. The picturesque houses which are scattered along the coast, and which are the homes of life-saving crews, are visited by thousands of people each year, and a great deal of curiosity as well as of interest is evinced in the methods of work of these brave men, as well as in their modes of life.

It may not occur to the average person who, perhaps, is accustomed to visit only one or two places on the extended coast-line of this country, how extensive the life saving service is, and how large an amount of money is expended each year by the general government in maintaining it. While the total expenditure amounts to nearly one million dollars annually, still there is no one who believes the public money is being expended in a too lavish manner in this particular at least.

The steady growth of the service is an evidence that the representatives of the people in Congress assembled appreciate the importance and value of the work accomplished by the hardy men who man our life-stations. It may, perhaps, be concluded that the provisions made for this service is hardly adequate, especially when it is considered that the sea and lake coasts of the United States, exclusive of the coasts of Alaska, have an extent of more than 10,000 miles.

To give succor to the vessels which may be tossed upon the rocks or stranded upon the shores of this extensive coast-line, there are only 226 life-saving stations, 165 of which are on the shores of the Atlantic, 8 on the Gulf of Mexico, 8 on the shores the pacific, and 45 on the shores of the Great Lakes. There is, besides, a station at the falls of the Ohio river at Louisville, Ky. The points selected are the most dangerous, and where the vessels, especially those engaged in the coasting trade, are exposed to storms.

They receive a compensation of $50 per month during the active season which on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts extend from the first day of September in each year until the first day of the succeeding May and those on the lake coasts from the opening to the close of navigation. Some of the stations on the Pacific coast are kept open the year round. Beyond the wages mentioned, the surfmen, as the men at the stations are known, receive no allowance except the quarters and fuel provided at the station.

In case of disability which continues for not more than a year, the surfmen is entitled to receive full pay and in case of death by reason of injury or disease incurred in the line of his duty, his widow or children under sixteen years of age may receive for two years the pay that deceased would have if alive.

During the season a day watch is maintained as well a nigh patrol, and on stated days the men are required to go through a boat and apparatus drill in order to keep familiar with their duties.

Each station is provided with a life boat, which is known as the life boat, of which there are several varieties in use. They are so light as to be readily transported along the shore; they can be launched in very shallow water, and in experienced hands can be handled in the breakers with marvelous ease and celerity. In cases where the surf boat cannot be used a line is shot out to the distressed vessel from a gun which has been especially provided for this purpose, and on this line a vehicle is sent from the shore to transport the people from the wreck.

Each station is provided with the facilities for caring for those who have been rescued, and a store of medicine as well as of clothes is kept on hand.

Since the service was put into operation in its present form in 1871 to the close of that year, there have been nearly 5,000 disasters, the value of the property involved being over $81,000,000. Through the efficiency of

the service over $60,000,000 of this property was saved, while of the 43,000 persons whose lives were imperiled only 505 were lost. During this period of twenty-four years the cost of maintaining the service was $9,000,000.

Take it upon a calculation of what it pays to-day, and I assert, and assert boldly, and agree never to make this race if the State of Kentucky is not out of debt and not owing one dollar, if you will convert that property at its present value according to the dividends it is paying, put it into money and pay off the debt.

Why, he says for seventeen years we left the negroes without any school provisions. I say that is not true; that long, long before that, that immediately after the war, the State of Kentucky generously gave to the negroes of the State every dollar of taxation that came off their own property. It supported them and it took care of them; it provided them with government, and then it generously turned around and gave every dollar off of their taxation to them in schools. My time is up. I wanted to answer some of those questions; I will answer them.
bob-haggard-ford-1895-07-16.A19:
VICTIMS OF MOB LAW.
One Hundred and Four People Murdered Since March Last.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN—Sir: The frequency with which acts of lawlessness on the part of mobs in all parts of the country are recorded in the daily newspapers has very materially blunted the public conscience into indifference to the gravity of the situation in this respect. The every-day report of mob violence does not appear to disturb the public conscience. It is taken and regarded as one of the stereotyped features of the news of the day. The murder of a citizen by his fellow citizens banded together as a mob does not apparently affect the general opinion of those whose business it is to create and control public opinion. And yet all law-abiding citizens admit that the orderly administration of the laws is the only safeguard that society has against demoralization, and that the only way to deal with criminals is by regular legal process.

It is only when the mob oversteps the bounds of humanity, as in the murder of the eleven Italians by the people of New Orleans, or the torturing and burning in a public square of a half-witted negro by the people of Paris, Texas, that the public conscience shows a disposition to resent the obtrusion of mobocracy as a central force in the government of society.

Crime thrives upon what it feeds. It proceeds from one excess to another by gradual stages, seeking always novelty in its methods. By gradual stages it progresses until a climax is reached beyond which it does not seem possible to go. The Paris incident was of this character. It was an incident for which there can be no apology or excuse.

The best men of the place justified it, however, upon grounds of public necessity, and abused everybody who did not accept their views of the situation. But there is no doubt in the minds of any one that the people of Paris who participated in that horrid crime will never recover from the degrading influence of it.

The New Orleans incident produced an international complication. Some Italians had been murdered in cold blood. They were in the hands of the law and legal authority. The evidence against them was sufficient to convict them or exonerate them. But the citizens of New Orleans, acting upon an impulse of madness, undertook to take the law of the State into their own hands, and in doing so violated a vital principle of international law and risked a war with a friendly power. This was averted only by the payment to the aggrieved of an indemnity, in the payment of which Louisiana had only an indirect part. It refused as a corporate body to give any satisfaction to the State Department at Washington or to the Italian Foreign Office. To preserve the good relations of the Federal Government to a friendly foreign power, the United States were compelled to pay the $20,000 demanded by justice. The whole people of the country were compelled to pay for the lawlessness of a single State.

In the August number of the Basis, Judge Albion W. Tourgee estimates the number of mob murders from March 1, 1895, to Aug. 1 to be 104. This is a fearful number of people to be slaughtered outside of the pale of the law. The crimes for which these people were murdered are entirely irrelevant as an excuse. Criminals are supposed to be innocent in the eye of the law until they are proven to be guilty as charged, and the verdict of no mob, however respectable the elements which compose it, can be taken as a sufficient warrant for its lawlessness. Judge Tourgee gives the following record for the month of July alone, and it is sufficient to shock the moral sense of Christian mankind:

Marshall E. Price, Denton, Md., July 2, hanged, colored, male; murder. Two, names unknown, Guthrie, O.T., July 2, nanged, white, males; horse stealing. John Barnwell, Edgefield, S. C., July 3, shot, colored, male, by four white boys; no excuse given. The Rev. Robert Bennett, Lake City, Fla., July 4, shot, colored; said to have attempted outrage on white woman. Theodore Puckett, Pelahatchie Creek, Miss., July 4, hanged, colored, male; charged with stealing money. Thomas Parker, Baldwin county, Miss., July 4, hanged, colored, male; charged with stealing watch. Joseph Howton, Princeton, Ky., July 4, shot, white, male; no excuse given. Howlet Howton, Princeton, Ky., July 4, shot, white, male; no excuse given. William Walker, New Orleans, La., July 9, white, male, shot by posse; said to be a desperado. Scot Vaughn, New Orleans, La., July 10, shot, colored, male; did not want ditch dug in front of his own house. Two men, names not known, Hampton, Ark., July 13, hanged, colored, males; accused of murder. Bob Haggard, Winchester, Ky., July 14, hanged, colored, m
riot at Brookside Mines, Ala. John Tinsley, Meridian, Miss., July 14, shot, colored, male; interfered to prevent colored woman being chastised. Mary Hunley, white, Cora Pace, colored, and Lewis Stewart, white, July 10, whipped; charged with adultery; taken out of jail, given 100 lashes, then returned to jail. Summary: Total, 37; total killed, 31; shot through shoulder, 1; whipped, 5; white, 6; colored, 31; hanged, 11; shot to death, 20; males, 32; females, 5.

The tendency to lynch law violence is constantly on the increase. That public sentiment in certain centres is largely against sustaining the officers of the law as against a mob is borne out by the Roanoke incident, where, after protecting his prisoner by firing into the mob, the military officer was compelled to flee from the place, as well as the Mayor. A similar condition of affairs recently developed in an Ohio town. Four men were recently lynched in California. There have been three lynchings in Ohio within the year, and one at least in Iowa. It is a very dull day in the South when some man is not swung up to a tree and riddled with bullets, charged with some alleged offence against law and order and decency, and who could more wisely and safely be turned over to the lawful authorities to be punished in the usual and proper way. The history of the Paris Commune teaches that the mob cannot be relied upon to do other than destroy life and property and to subvert government. The reign of the mob in the United States is gaining a firmer hold every year, and it behooves those who believe in law and order to face it resolutely and fight it down.

NEW YORK, Aug. 30. T. THOMAS FORTUNE.

OVER A WOMAN.
White Man and a Negro Engage in Fatal Quarrel.
Cincinnati, Aug.12.—Yesterday Thomas Jones, colored, and James Daly, White, met at the room of Emma Conley, white. Daly Drove Jones away. Today Jones visited the woman, with another negro, Henry Williams. He attacked Daly and stabbed him. He and Williams then ran out, but officers caught Jones and a mob of 300 took after Williams. The officers had to show their pistols to keep back the crowd.
henry-williams-cincinnati-1895-08-11.A2:
Negro Chased by a Mob.
CINCINNATI, O., Aug. 12.—Yesterday Thomas Jones, colored, and James Daley, white, met at the room of Mary Conley, white. Daley drove Jones away. To-day Jones visited the woman with another negro, Henry Williams. He attacked Daley and fatally stabbed him. He and Williams then ran out, but officers caught Jones and a mob of three hundred people took after Williams. While running, Williams grabbed bricks, which he hurled back into the crowd. At the depot fully two thousand people surrounded him and a brakeman knocked him down with a bowlder. The officers had to show their pistols to keep the crowd back.

Crimes and Casualties.
Human blood was found in Holmes' castle in Chicago bespattered from one room to another by Detectives Fitzpatrick and Norton.

Miss Carrie Hart was thrown from a wagonette by a runaway team at Henderson, Ky., and killed after she had heroically saved the life of a child by lowering it to the ground.

There were two deaths from heat at Akron, O., Saturday.

Isaac Watson, farmer, was killed by sunstroke near Georgetown, O.

At Perry, O. T., Ben Cravens, Bill Crittenden, two noted United States prisoners, broke jail and were pursued by a posse and Cravens killed.

Zeke Bryon, who killed a guard at the Kingston (Tenn.) convict camp June 27 and escaped, has been recaptured and brought to Nashville.

Laborers discovered three bodies in the ruins of the collapsed building at New York yesterday. They were so battered and mutilated as to be beyond identification.

Simon Kostead and his son, Edward, were frightfully hacked and stabbed by William Rose, a burly negro at Kalamazoo, Mich.

James Daley, white, was fatally stabbed by Thomas Jones, colored, at Cincinnati.

Night Marshal William Shea was shot and killed at Victor, Colo., by three deputy sheriffs.

Five men and one woman were injured by an explosion in a canning factory at Longmont, Colo.

The condition of Russell H. Conwell, the Philadelphia divine, taken sick at Youngstown, O., has improved.

The stage which left Oregon City, Or., yesterday morning was held up by masked men and the passengers relieved of all their money and valuables.

james-burns-sylvania-1895-08-03.A1:
A DESPERATE FIGHT.
An Alleged Murderer Fires Eight Shots at the Officers.
Sylvania, Ga., Aug. 3.—A lively battle occurred on the outskirts of our town yesterday afternoon about sundown, between a desperate colored criminal by the name of James Burns and Messrs. Will Kemp and Julius Arnett, who were after him to arrest him. Sixteen shots were fired—eight on each side, and although hit seven times, the negro fought desperately until he was knocked in the head with a rifle, after which he fell upon his face and died in a few moments. Neither of the two white men were hit, notwithstanding they were shot at eight times, mostly at close quarters.

Burns killed another negro here two years ago, on account of jealousy about a woman; the deed was done in cold blood, and the murderer escaped. Yesterday afternoon Constable Bob Bazemore accidentally struck up with Burns near a little negro house just out of town, and cajoled with him until he got one of his pistols away from him, ostensibly to look at it. He then ordered Burns to throw up his hands and march before him toward Sylvania; this the negro reluctantly did, until, watching his opportunity, he sprang back upon the constable and wrenching the pistol from his grasp, ordered the officer to clear out, or he would blow his head off. There was nothing for Bazemore to do but comply, but as soon as the negro was at a safe distance he sent up town for Sheriff Brooker, who went down to the scene, accompanied by Kemp and Arnett. Burns had not left the negro house, and when he saw the party approaching he ran out across the woods to escape. Kemp and Arnett followed him, and the latter ran around the branch to cut him off. As soon as they got out in a clear space the negro turned and commenced firing on Kemp. Kemp reciprocated with a rifle and shot the darkey through the head the first fire. Then the fusilade became general. The negro emptied all but one ball out of his two pistols at his pursuers and then clinched with Arnett, who had headed him off. With terrible desperation, and even then in the agony of death, he was attempting to shoot Arnett, and would probably have done so had not Kemp come up and felled him with the rifle. It was found that out of eight shots fired at him he had been hit seven times—five with the pistol and two with the rifle. He did not hurt either of his pursuers, although the bullets whistled uncomfortably close to their heads.

Eleven Bullets Killed Him.
Eleven Bullets Killed Him.
Sylvania, Ga., Aug. 7.—News of a sensational battle between officers and a desperate criminal has reached here. James Burns about two years ago killed Frank Bender on account of jealousy of a woman. He escaped, and for two years has been in hiding. Yesterday he was discovered in a swamp near here, and a gang of deputy sheriffs started out to capture him. In the battle which took place Burns received eleven bullets in his body and died soon after.
